01 · Foundations

What is Agent?

An agent is a model that plans, remembers, and acts on the world through tools — wrapped in controls and logging.

An agent pairs a reasoning model with the machinery to act: instructions that guide decisions, memory to retrieve and store context, and tools (often via protocols like MCP) to interact with external systems.

What makes it production-grade is the layer underneath: controls — access controls, guardrails, and human approvals — and logging & monitoring over everything it does. Capability without these is just exposure.

Ref · IMDA Model Governance Framework for Agentic AI
imda.gov.sg/…/mgf-for-agentic-ai.pdf
Anatomy of an agent — model · memory · tools · protocols, under controls & logging
02 · Risk Model

Agent Risk & Blast Radius

Two independent axes define how much damage an agent can do: how autonomously it acts, and which environment it can reach.

Autonomy (left) × environment reach (right) — controls scale with the corner you're in

An agent in a sandbox with low autonomy has very low risks. A fully autonomous agent in production production is the opposite corner — the blast radius depends on what it can do.

The rule of thumb

Risk = Threat × Impact × Vulnerability — and both axes feed it: more autonomy raises the threat and vulnerability, a wider environment raises the impact. Map every agent to its corner, then scale controls to the risk before you ship it.

03 · Communication · Human → Agent

Who talks to the agent, and why

Common human to agent use cases

Persona · User

Acting on my behalf

  • Agent represents the human for routine actions (e.g. a $100 transfer within limit)
  • Human-in-the-loop kicks in past a threshold (e.g. a $1,000 transfer above limit)
Persona · Infrastructure

Provisioning (AIOps)

  • Spin up / tear down environments on request
Persona · Developer

Developer Workflow

  • Coding agent — from IDE to pipeline
  • Use it for troubleshooting
  • Apply baseline security by default — e.g. agentic AI checks, or guardrails like no secrets pushed to GitHub
Persona · Security

Investigate & respond, Governance

  • Investigate / triage alerts — confirm whether an alert is a real incident
  • Respond to incidents — isolate a host, revoke a token, force a reset (high blast-radius, HITL)
  • Compliance evidence — gather it for a control ahead of an audit
  • Check audit logs to identify who accessed what
Note on governance · the common pattern

Across all four personas it’s the same pattern — every one reduces to four questions: Who is acting · with whom Consent · to do What · for How long. That shift is exactly what governance has to account for next.

03 · Communication · Agent → Agent

Why do agent talk to agent?

Common multi-agent use cases

USE CASE 01

Conversational questions and answers

Chatbot. A common example we see is an employee accessing company chatbot for FAQs or support. The agent may route it to other specialist agent to complete a task.

USE CASE 02

Operations

Agents are embedded in operational workflows to automate routine tasks and improve efficiency. Example: automating insurance claims processing

USE CASE 03

Automated troubleshooting and triaging

Detection, diagnosis, and remediation split across agents to reduce mean time to resolution. Example: Security SOC, Production troubleshooting

When it's worth it · and the bridge to governance

Reach for multi-agent when decomposition improves quality, focus, and safety — accepting the added latency and token cost. It also enables context management: pass each specialist only the minimum context for better focus, lower token load, and less data exposure. At each hop, escalate to a human on over-limit or irreversible actions, low confidence, or policy violations — which is exactly where governance takes over.

Ref · Anthropic — Building effective agents
anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents
04 · Governance · The Problem

Four critical risk areas

Left unchecked, agentic access fails in four predictable ways — the gaps the imperatives that follow are built to close.

RISK 01

Over-privilege without visibility

Agents accumulate standing access far beyond need — a massive blast radius if compromised.

RISK 02

No real-time enforcement

The last mile is unguarded when agents invoke tools and APIs — end-to-end security breaks.

RISK 03

Impersonation & invisible delegation

User impersonation breaks audit trails. You can't answer: “Who authorized this?”

RISK 04

Zero accountability

New models ship without proper access and compliance controls in place.

From problem to practice

As agents act on behalf of humans, security shifts from securing infrastructure to governing the agents themselves — the new question is not just who did something, but which agent did it, on whose behalf, and under what authority. Five imperatives close these gaps →

Ref · HashiCorp — Agentic runtime security: solving agentic AI identity & access gaps
hashicorp.com/…/agentic-runtime-security-solving-agentic-ai-identity-and-access-gaps
04 · Governance · The Response

Five implementation imperatives

As agents act on behalf of humans, security shifts from securing infrastructure to governing the agents — which agent did it, on whose behalf, and under what authority. Five imperatives make that real.

1

Register every agent

Unique, verifiable, cryptographically bound identity. No shared keys or credentials.

2

Strip standing privileges

Just-in-time, scoped access. Authority expires automatically.

3

Tie actions to intent

Capture consent, purpose, sponsorship. Traceable and instantly revocable.

4

Enforce at point of use

Every API call validated against policy. Nothing executes outside boundaries.

5

Produce proof of control

Audit trail answers in seconds. Cryptographically signed evidence.

Underneath every demo · Governance

The Security persona isn't a separate demo — it's the layer running under all three. Every action answers the same four questions: Who is acting (agent identity, on whose behalf) · with what Consent · to do What (scoped to intent) · and for How long (short-lived, auto-expiring authority). That's how each walkthrough stays accountable.
